questions.question: Which patient is included in the USPSTF recommendation for osteoporosis screening?
choices: A woman age 65 years or older
Every adult regardless of risk
Only patients after hip fracture
No postmenopausal women
questions.explanation: USPSTF recommends osteoporosis screening for women 65 years or older and for younger postmenopausal women at increased risk.

questions.question: Why is a low-trauma fracture from standing height clinically important?
choices: It can be a fragility-fracture sentinel event requiring bone-health and fall-risk evaluation
It has no implications after acute care
It proves every fracture is traumatic
It replaces the need to assess falls
questions.explanation: A low-trauma fracture can indicate elevated future fracture risk and should trigger comprehensive prevention follow-up.

questions.question: What does a DXA T-score provide?
choices: A bone-density comparison with a young-adult reference population
A complete measure of all fracture risk
A diagnosis of every secondary cause
A replacement for fracture history
questions.explanation: T-scores help assess bone density but do not replace clinical fracture, fall, or secondary-cause assessment.

questions.question: Which history increases concern for secondary osteoporosis?
choices: Long-term glucocorticoid exposure or endocrine/renal/malabsorption disease
A stable normal gait
A remote uncomplicated cold
Correct medication adherence
questions.explanation: Medication exposure and endocrine, renal, malabsorptive, inflammatory, cancer-related, and other conditions can contribute to secondary osteoporosis.

questions.question: Which intervention is part of fracture prevention?
choices: Assess falls, gait, vision, home hazards, medications, balance, and mobility
Only recommend a supplement
Avoid all activity
Ignore sedating medications
questions.explanation: Fall prevention requires multifactorial assessment and individualized mobility, home, and medication interventions.

questions.question: Why should osteoporosis treatment be reassessed over time?
choices: Medication response, organ function, adherence, adverse effects, and transition needs can change
Treatment never needs monitoring
DXA eliminates every follow-up need
Only the prescription date matters
questions.explanation: Osteoporosis therapies differ in monitoring and discontinuation/transition needs, so ongoing reassessment is essential.

questions.question: Which presentation requires urgent evaluation for possible fracture complication?
choices: Inability to bear weight after a fall with hip pain
Stable preventive counseling visit
Improved balance after therapy
A routine medication refill
questions.explanation: Hip pain and inability to bear weight after a fall may indicate a serious fracture requiring urgent assessment.

questions.question: Why should new severe back pain with height loss be evaluated promptly?
choices: It may represent a vertebral compression fracture
It always reflects normal aging
It proves supplements are working
It is unrelated to bone health
questions.explanation: New severe back pain and height loss can indicate vertebral fracture and warrant timely evaluation.

questions.question: What is an important therapy-safety question before changing an osteoporosis medication?
choices: What is the indication, administration plan, organ function, adverse-effect context, and transition consequence?
Can the medication be continued without assessing therapy transition?
Can follow-up be omitted?
Does every patient use the same agent?
questions.explanation: Safe treatment changes require understanding the drug’s purpose, monitoring, administration, and transition risks.

questions.question: What is the FNP-level osteoporosis principle?
choices: Treat bone density as an isolated number
Integrate fracture history, secondary causes, DXA/risk, falls, therapy safety, function, and access
Screen every person the same way
Wait until a second fracture to act
questions.explanation: High-quality osteoporosis care aims to prevent future fracture through individualized, coordinated bone and fall-risk care.
